extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientifically literate scholars and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating the criteria by which paradigms differ, how they guide scientific practice, and what counts as legitimate problems, methods, and solutions across scientific revolutions. Intended for analysis of paradigm change and its epistemic/behavioral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive differences between successive paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive paradigms tell us different things about the population of the universe and about that population’s behavior (for example, the existence of subatomic particles, the materiality of light, and the conservation of heat or of energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are substantive differences that require no further illustration; they are necessary and irreconcilable and constitute one primary mode in which paradigms differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms direct methods, problem-fields, and standards of solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms are the source of the methods, problem-field, and standards of solution accepted by any mature scientific community at any given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reception of a new paradigm often necessitates a redefinition of the corresponding science: some old problems may be relegated to another science or declared unscientific; previously trivial or non-existent problems may become central; standards that distinguish scientific solutions from mere speculation change accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards that distinguish scientific solution from metaphysical or mathematical play
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paradigm establishes standards that distinguish a real scientific solution from a mere metaphysical speculation, word game, or mathematical play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When paradigms change these standards change too, and the normal-scientific tradition emerging after a revolution is often incompatible or incommensurable with the previous one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Older theories convertible to successors only via hindsight-driven transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: An out-of-date theory can always be viewed as a special case of its up-to-date successor only if it is transformed for the purpose, and that transformation can be undertaken only with the advantages of hindsight and the explicit guidance of the more recent theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such transformed restatements may have economy and limited utility but cannot serve to guide active research in the way the current paradigm does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-cumulative and reversible nature of changes in problems and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in problems and standards induced by paradigm shifts are not necessarily cumulative improvements; they can be reversed and are not objectively higher or lower without external criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no external neutral standards to judge whether one set of standards is intrinsically superior; what changes is demanded by adopting a new paradigm, and later developments can revert standards (examples: attempts to explain gravity; chemical explanations of qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as constitutive of research activity (map + directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the theories they embody, paradigms are constitutive of research activity: they tell the scientist about entities and behaviors (a map) and provide directions essential for map-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because nature is too complex to be explored at random, paradigms (maps plus directions) are as essential as observation and experiment for science's continuing development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory, methods, and standards acquired together
rubrics_metrics.description: In learning a paradigm the scientist acquires theory, methods, and standards together, usually in an inextricable mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, paradigm change typically brings significant shifts in the criteria determining the legitimacy of both problems and proposed solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incommensurability of paradigm debates and need for external (non-normal) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Because paradigms define what counts as a problem and what counts as a solution, competing paradigms will often talk through each other: each will satisfy its own criteria and fail some of the other's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution requires recourse to criteria outside normal science (values, priorities); this recourse is what makes paradigm debates revolutionary rather than decidable by normal-scientific standards alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-induced perceptual (gestalt) shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: When paradigms change, scientists may 'see' the same instruments or phenomena differently — a shift analogous to gestalt-reversal (duck/rabbit) or to visual adaptation (inverting goggles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These perceptual changes mean that after a revolution scientists may literally and figuratively respond to a different world; examples include astronomers seeing planets/comets differently, or Lavoisier seeing oxygen where predecessors saw dephlogisticated air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of direct testimonial evidence for perceptual shifts — rely on indirect behavioral evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike psychological subjects who can switch perception back and forth and be externally corrected, scientists cannot appeal to a higher authority to demonstrate a perceptual switch; thus scientists rarely attest directly to having seen differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians must look for indirect and behavioral evidence (changes in classification, discovery patterns, instruments used, new phenomena identified) to infer paradigm-induced perceptual transformations (examples: Herschel’s detection of Uranus; later discovery rates of asteroids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reclassification of phenomena and instruments under new paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a new paradigm previously salient features may be re-described and different aspects emphasized (e.g., Leyden jar reinterpreted as a 'condenser' emphasizing two conducting coatings; devices reconceived as metal plates separated by a non-conductor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigm change alters which properties and parts of instruments are seen as central, leads to new prototypes and conceptual classes, and enables new phenomena to be noted and studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception depends on training; paradigms as prerequisites to seeing
rubrics_metrics.description: What a person sees depends both on what he looks at and on what his previous visual-conceptual experience has taught him to see; without such training perception is a 'bloomin' buzzin' confusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific training inculcates paradigms (conceptual categories) that allow the scientist to 'see' discipline-specific entities and regularities; thus becoming a scientist involves learning new perceptual/conceptual categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm change affects which problems are judged significant to have solved
rubrics_metrics.description: Because no paradigm solves all the problems it defines and no two paradigms leave exactly the same problems unsolved, debates between paradigms involve the question 'Which problems is it more significant to have solved?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answering that question requires values and priorities external to normal science, contributing to the revolutionary character of paradigm choice.
